name: The Art of War
info: The Art of War is an ancient Chinese military treatise in 13 chapters, attributed to Sun Tzu and dated to the late Spring and Autumn period, roughly the 5th century BCE; it later headed the Seven Military Classics.

facts.made: Attributed by tradition to the strategist Sun Tzu (Sun Wu) of the state of Qi, said to have served King Helü of Wu; the earlier text was probably completed between 500 and 430 BCE
facts.form: A Chinese military treatise in 13 chapters (piān), counted as one zhuàn, written on bamboo slips in its earliest surviving copies
facts.where: Read in many editions and translations; the Yinqueshan Han slips, with an early copy of the text, were found in two tombs near Linyi in Shandong
facts.known: War as a costly last resort; keeping war brief and cheap; diplomacy and economy in strategy; espionage and intelligence; the Seven Military Classics; readers from Takeda Shingen to Mao Zedong and Võ Nguyên Giáp

t: The treatise treats war as a costly and destructive last resort and teaches how to keep it brief, contained and cheap, with a stress on diplomacy, economic principles and intelligence.

Its author is disputed: tradition names Sun Tzu of the 6th century BCE, while scholars have doubted that he existed, and the 1972 Yinqueshan slips showed that two related texts bore the name of Master Sun.
For almost 1,500 years it was the lead text of an anthology formalised in 1080 as the Seven Military Classics, and it has been read by military and political leaders in East Asia and the West.
dyk: The earliest known commentary on the text, written by a strategist and warlord in the early 3rd century, comes with a preface admitting that he edited the book and removed certain passages; how much he changed has never been clear.
ev: Sun Tzu, the traditional author, is said to have lived in this century
The earlier text of The Art of War is now generally accepted as completed between 500 and 430 BCE
Two Han tombs near Linyi in Shandong are sealed between 134 and 118 BCE with bamboo slips that include the Sun Tzu text
A strategist and warlord writes the earliest known commentary and edits the text
Emperor Shenzong of Song formalises the Seven Military Classics, with The Art of War at their head
The French Jesuit Jean Joseph Marie Amiot produces the first translation into a European language
Lionel Giles publishes the first annotated English translation
The Yinqueshan Han slips are discovered in the two tombs near Linyi

sections.origins:
The Art of War is a military treatise of ancient China, dated to the late Spring and Autumn period, roughly the 5th century BCE. The period itself is given as 776 to 471 BCE. Tradition attributes the work to a general known as Sun Tzu (pinyin Sūnzǐ), 'Master Sun', who is said to have lived in the 6th century BCE, although the earliest parts of the text probably date to at least 100 years later. Sima Qian's Shiji, the first of China's Twenty-Four Histories, records an early Chinese tradition that a text on military matters was written by one Sun Wu (孫武) from the state of Qi, and that King Helü of Wu (r. 514–495 BCE) had read and studied it. This text was traditionally identified with the received Master Sun's Art of War.

The conventional view was that Sun Wu was a military theorist from the end of the Spring and Autumn period who fled Qi to the southeastern state of Wu. There he is said to have impressed the king with his ability to quickly train officials, including court women, in military discipline, and to have made the armies of Wu powerful enough to challenge the rival state of Chu to the west. This view is still widely held in China. The treatise itself comprises a detailed explanation and analysis of the 5th-century BCE Chinese military.
sections.content:
The Art of War is divided into thirteen chapters (piān), and the collection is referred to as one zhuàn, 'whole' or alternatively 'chronicle'. Each chapter is devoted to a different set of skills or arts related to warfare, finance and how they apply to military strategy and tactics. The treatise ranges from weapons, environmental conditions, financial logistics and strategy to morale, rank and discipline.

Sun portrays war as a costly, destructive last resort. Prolonged warfare erodes the state faster than the enemy ever could. He uses diplomacy and economic principles to explain how to keep war brief, contained, controlled and as cheap as possible by minimising financial exposure. He also stresses the importance of intelligence operatives and espionage, both to the war effort and to the prevention of war.

Two passages are quoted in the sources on the book's use. One, which Mao Zedong cited, runs 'Know your enemy and know yourself and you can fight a hundred battles without disaster.' The other, a strategy of deception that some authors say the KGB studied, runs 'I will force the enemy to take our strength for weakness, and our weakness for strength, and thus will turn his strength into weakness'.
sections.making:
Who made the text is disputed. Beginning around the 12th century, Chinese scholars began to question Sun Tzu's historical existence. Their main ground was that the Zuo Zhuan, which mentions most of the notable figures of the Spring and Autumn period, does not mention him at all, and the name Sun Wu does not appear in any text before the Records of the Grand Historian. Some scholars have suspected it is a made-up descriptive nickname meaning 'the fugitive warrior'. In the early 20th century the writer and reformer Liang Qichao theorised that the text was written in the 4th century BCE by Sun Tzu's purported descendant Sun Bin, as several historical sources mention a military treatise he wrote. Samuel B. Griffith held it possible that Sun Wu may not have written The Art of War.

The discovery of the Yinqueshan Han slips in 1972 changed the argument. Two separate texts were found in two Han tombs near Linyi in Shandong, sealed between 134 and 118 BCE: one attributed to Sun Tzu, corresponding to the received text, and another attributed to Sun Bin, which explains and expands upon the earlier work. The content of the earlier text is about one-third of the chapters of the modern book, and its text matches very closely. It is now generally accepted that the earlier Art of War was completed sometime between 500 and 430 BCE.
sections.reception:
For almost 1,500 years The Art of War was the lead text in an anthology that Emperor Shenzong of Song formalised in 1080 as the Seven Military Classics. Across East Asia it was part of the syllabus for candidates in military service examinations. In the Sengoku period (c. 1467–1568) the Japanese daimyō Takeda Shingen (1521–1573) is said to have become almost invincible in all battles without relying on guns because he studied it, and the book is said to have given him the inspiration for his battle standard Fūrinkazan (Wind, Forest, Fire and Mountain), meaning fast as the wind, silent as a forest, ferocious as fire and immovable as a mountain.

In the 20th century the translator Samuel B. Griffith cited it as an influence on Mao Zedong's On Guerrilla Warfare, On the Protracted War and Strategic Problems of China's Revolutionary War. During the Vietnam War some Viet Cong officers studied it extensively and reportedly could recite entire passages from memory, and General Võ Nguyên Giáp, an avid student of Sun Tzu's ideas, is said to have implemented tactics described in it at the Battle of Dien Bien Phu. Douglas MacArthur is quoted as saying that he always kept a copy on his desk, and Colin Powell as saying that it continues to influence both soldiers and politicians.
sections.survival:
The text reached later ages through copying, editing and commentary. A strategist and warlord wrote the earliest known commentary in the early 3rd century. His preface makes clear that he edited the text and removed certain passages, but the extent of his changes was unclear historically. The Art of War appears throughout the bibliographical catalogues of the Chinese dynastic histories, but the listings of its divisions and size varied widely.

The bamboo slips found at Yinqueshan in 1972 gave scholars an early copy to set beside the received text, and showed that much of the historical confusion arose because two texts could have been called Master Sun's Art of War, not one. One scholarly suggestion is that the two may be 'a single, continuously developing intellectual tradition united under the Sun name'.

The text was first translated into a European language in 1772, when the French Jesuit priest Jean Joseph Marie Amiot produced a French version. The first annotated English translation, by the British scholar Lionel Giles, was published in 1910. Later translators include Samuel B. Griffith (1963), Thomas Cleary (1988), Roger Ames (1993), John Minford (2002), Victor H. Mair (2007) and Michael Nylan (2020).
sections.legacy:
The Art of War remains one of the most influential works on strategy and has shaped both East Asian and Western military theory. The United States' defeat in the Vietnam War, more than any other event, brought Sun Tzu to the attention of leaders of American military theory. The Command and General Staff College of the Department of the Army lists the book as one that may be kept in a military unit's library, and it is on the US Marine Corps Professional Reading Program. It is also used at the United States Military Academy and is recommended reading for officer cadets at the Royal Military Academy, Sandhurst. Griffith's 1963 translation was published as part of the UNESCO Collection of Representative Works.

Admirers claim a wider range of uses for the book in competitive endeavours outside the military, among them espionage, politics, business, sport and law. Some Japanese companies make it required reading for their key executives, and it has been the subject of legal books and articles on negotiation and trial strategy. These are the claims of admirers and of business books, not established findings.

summary: The Art of War is an ancient Chinese treatise on strategy in 13 chapters, attributed to Sun Tzu and probably completed between 500 and 430 BCE. It treats war as a costly last resort, led the Seven Military Classics and has been read by commanders in East Asia and the West.
references: Samuel Griffith, Sun Tzu: The Illustrated Art of War (Oxford University Press, 2005)
Victor H. Mair, The Art of War: Sun Zi's Military Methods (Columbia University Press, 2007)
Derek M. C. Yuen, Deciphering Sun Tzu: How to Read 'The Art of War' (Oxford University Press, 2014)
notes: Authorship: the article reports the traditional Sun Wu of Qi, the doubts since the 12th century, Liang Qichao's Sun Bin theory and the Yinqueshan finds; I reported each as held by its holder and gave no verdict. 'Earliest parts probably date to at least 100 years later' than the 6th century and 'completed 500-430 BCE' are both the article's; start is -500 circa.
The article says the earlier text's content is about one-third of the chapters of the modern book; I did not say which chapters.
Left out: film, television, game, sport and e-book references (guide rule), and the unsupported detail of what each of the 13 chapters is about, which the article does not give.
The article lists Mao's quote as 'Sun Wu Tzu' with a hundred-battles line; the KGB deception quote is given with 'according to some authors'. Both are attributed accordingly.
Giáp's use at Dien Bien Phu is given by the article as 'successfully implemented tactics described in The Art of War'; I wrote 'is said to have'.
The 'where' fact for the Yinqueshan slips gives the find site only; the article names no museum.
The facts 'form' mentions bamboo slips for the earliest surviving copies: the article says bamboo slip writings were found in the tombs.
